replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a surprise: an LLM never sees your words. It only ever sees numbers.

Before your prompt goes anywhere, it gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, which are chunks of text, sometimes whole words and sometimes fragments. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of them, and each token is swapped for a number.

[KEY]Your prompt is converted from words into tokens, and tokens into numbers, before the model does anything with it.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine a tokenizer that splits "unbelievable" into "un", "believ", and "able". Each piece gets its own number (say 412, 9087, 553 — made up for illustration, since real tokenizers use different IDs). The model works only with that list of numbers.[/EX]

[Q]
Which statement best describes what the model receives when you type a prompt?
A) A list of numbers standing in for chunks of text
B) The exact letters you typed, one at a time
C) Whole sentences it matches against stored answers
D) Images of your words that it reads visually
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) A list of numbers standing in for chunks of text
replies.raw:
Right, a list of numbers standing in for chunks of text. That's the only thing the model ever works with.

Now for what it does with those numbers. The model's one job is to **predict the next token**: given everything so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary by how likely it is to come next.

Take "The cat sat on the ___". Almost everything points to one answer ("mat" or "floor" or "couch"), so the model is highly confident about its top choices. But after "My favorite thing to do on a weekend is ___", thousands of continuations fit, so the probability is spread thin.

[KEY]The model doesn't look up an answer. It scores every possible next token and picks from the likeliest ones, one token at a time.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine the model is given "The capital of France is ___". One token, "Paris", gets nearly all the probability. For "I'm in the mood for ___", the probability is spread across dozens of tokens like "pizza", "music", "sleep", and "adventure", with no clear winner. (Made-up scenarios, just to show the contrast.)[/EX]

[Q]
Why would a model be MORE confident predicting the next word after "Roses are red, violets are ___" than after "I want to eat ___"?
A) One continuation is far more common than all others
B) The word "violets" is a rarer token than "eat"
C) It looked the poem up in a database of verses
D) Shorter sentences always produce more confident predictions
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) The word "violets" is a rarer token than "eat"
replies.raw:
Not quite, and it's a tempting pick. How rare a token is doesn't decide confidence. What matters is how many different continuations would fit.

After "Roses are red, violets are ___", the poem is so familiar that one word ("blue") dominates the probabilities. After "I want to eat ___", dozens of words fit about equally well, so the probability gets spread thin. The model is confident when one answer clearly wins and unsure when many answers compete.

[KEY]Confidence comes from how lopsided the probabilities are: one dominant continuation means high confidence, many plausible ones means low confidence.[/KEY]

Let's try the same idea from a different angle.

[Q]
Which blank would the model be MOST confident about?
A) "Yesterday I felt really ___"
B) "Two plus two equals ___"
C) "The best movie ever made is ___"
D) "My best friend's name is ___"
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) "Two plus two equals ___"
replies.raw:
Yes, "four" dominates, while the other blanks have many fitting answers.

So far you've seen how the model turns words into numbers and then scores the likely next token. But a puzzle remains: the same token can mean different things. Take "bank", which gets the same token whether it's about money or a river.

The model handles this with two tools. First, each token becomes a long list of numbers called an **embedding**, which places words with similar meanings near each other. Second, **attention** lets the other words in the sentence adjust that embedding, so context decides which meaning wins.

[KEY]Attention lets surrounding words reshape a token's meaning, which is how the model tells one "bank" from another.[/KEY]

[EX]In "I sat on the bank of the river", attention links "bank" to "river", pulling it toward the shoreline meaning. In "I put cash in the bank", "cash" pulls it toward the money meaning. Same token, different result.[/EX]

[Q]
In "I put cash in the bank", what lets the model treat "bank" as a place for money?
A) The model remembers the word "bank" always means money
B) Other words in the sentence adjust its meaning
C) The model looks up "bank" in a dictionary first
D) The tokenizer assigns a different token for each meaning
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
replies.raw:
That's a precise way to put it, and it matches what you picked earlier: a dominant continuation means high confidence, and an open slot with several plausible words means low confidence.

But I asked a question first, and your message didn't pick an option. Here it is again:
